inline.s: [The Four Fearlessnesses] Fearlessness is a mind that knows no dread in teaching others. The Buddha has four fearlessnesses. First, fearlessness as to omniscience: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares himself to be the all-knowing one, with a mind free of fear. Second, fearlessness as to the extinction of the outflows: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares that he has utterly extinguished all defilements, with a mind free of fear. Third, fearlessness as to speaking of what obstructs the path: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares the various obstructive dharmas — delusion, karma, and the like — with a mind free of fear. Fourth, fearlessness as to speaking of the path that ends suffering: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares the true paths that end all suffering — precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth — with a mind free of fear.

[The Eighteen Unique Dharmas] These are the eighteen dharmas of merit that belong to the Buddha alone; because they are confined to the Buddha and are not shared by the three vehicles, they are called the “unique dharmas.” First, no error of body: since countless kalpas the Buddha has always cultivated his body through precepts, concentration, wisdom and compassion; because his merit is complete and all defilements are exhausted, this is called “no error of body.” Second, no error of speech: the Buddha possesses measureless wisdom and eloquence, and every word that issues from the Buddha’s golden mouth accords, character by character, with truth; this is called “no error of speech.” Third, no error of mindfulness: the Buddha possesses the supreme, profound and wondrous concentration; his mind is not scattered but abides constantly in samādhi, dwelling nowhere with regard to all dharmas; therefore this is called “no error of mindfulness.” Fourth, no differing thought: toward sentient beings the Buddha saves universally and equally, with a mind free of discrimination; this is called “no differing thought.” Fifth, no unsettled mind: whether walking, standing, sitting or lying down, the Buddha never departs from profound samādhi; this is called “no unsettled mind.” Sixth, no knowing-and-yet-abandoning: the Buddha teaches and saves sentient beings, saying whatever he knows with nothing left unsaid, and there is no dharma that he has understood and yet abandoned; this is called “no knowing-and-yet-abandoning.” Seventh, no diminishment of desire: the Buddha, compassionate toward sentient beings, desires to save them, and his mind knows no satiety; this is called “no diminishment of desire.” Eighth, no diminishment of vigor: the Buddha takes the salvation of all sentient beings as his own task, and so always saves them without rest; this is called “no diminishment of vigor.” Ninth, no diminishment of mindfulness: the Buddha’s dharmas and all the wisdoms of the Buddhas of the three times correspond and are complete without regression; this is called “no diminishment of mindfulness.” Tenth, no diminishment of wisdom: the Buddha possesses all wisdom, measureless and unbounded, beyond exhaustion; hence “no diminishment of wisdom.” Eleventh, no diminishment of liberation: the Buddha is far removed from all attachment and possesses two kinds of liberation — one is the conditioned liberation (the liberation that accords with undefiled wisdom), the other the unconditioned liberation (that in which all defilements are cleansed without remainder); this is called “no diminishment of liberation.” Twelfth, no diminishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation: within all liberations the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are clear and his discernment unobstructed; this is called “no diminishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.” Thirteenth, all bodily karma follows wisdom: all the Buddha’s bodily actions are led by wisdom, so that none lacks wisdom; this is called “all bodily karma following wisdom.” Fourteenth, all verbal karma follows wisdom: all the Buddha’s spoken words are likewise led by wisdom, so that none lacks wisdom; this is called “all verbal karma following wisdom.” Fifteenth, all mental karma follows wisdom: all the Buddha’s mental reflections are likewise led by wisdom, so that none lacks wisdom; this is called “all mental karma following wisdom.” Sixteenth, unobstructed wisdom knowing the past: the Buddha, with wisdom, illumines all the dharmas of the past and knows them universally without obstruction; this is called “unobstructed wisdom knowing the past.” Seventeenth, unobstructed wisdom knowing the future: the Buddha, with wisdom, illumines all things of the future and knows them universally without obstruction; this is called “unobstructed wisdom knowing the future.” Eighteenth, unobstructed wisdom knowing the present: the Buddha, with wisdom, illumines all things of the present and knows them universally without obstruction; this is called “unobstructed wisdom knowing the present.”

[Dragon King! Just as all cities, towns and villages rest upon the great earth and are securely established, and just as all medicinal herbs, plants, trees and thickets alike grow by relying upon the earth, so too are these ten wholesome karma paths. All humans and gods stand firm by depending on them; all the bodhi of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the practices of the bodhisattvas, and all the Buddha-dharma — together they rely upon this great earth of the ten wholesome karma paths and thereby are accomplished.]

The World-Honored One concluded, saying: Dragon King! Just as all cities, towns and villages rest upon the great earth and are securely established, and just as all medicinal herbs, plants, trees and thickets alike grow by relying upon the great earth, so too is it with these ten wholesome karma paths. All the human vehicle and the divine vehicle stand firm by depending on them; all the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, the bodhisattva vehicle, and all the Buddha-dharma together rely upon this great earth of the ten wholesome karma paths and thereby are accomplished.

[When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Dragon King Sāgara and the great assembly, together with all the gods, humans and asuras of the world, all greatly rejoiced and believed, received and practiced it.]

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, the Dragon King Sāgara and the assembly present at the Dharma gathering, together with all the gods, humans and asuras of the world, were all filled with the joy of the Dharma and believed, received and practiced it.
The key to gaining the benefit of reciting the sutras and hearing the Dharma lies in these four words: “believing, receiving and practicing.”

[Believing, receiving and practicing] Truly and sincerely believing and receiving the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, and earnestly putting into practice the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata. To hold and practice carries the sense of keeping it deeply in the heart — that is, never forgetting the Buddha’s words in a single thought, and never acting against the Buddha’s words in a single thought.

In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, the key is to grasp it for oneself and take it to heart. Take the Buddha’s words as a bright mirror, and reflect upon oneself at all times and in all places; take the Buddha’s words as a beacon, and advance according to the teachings. In one’s cultivation one must firmly grasp these three links — hearing, reflecting and practicing — bringing hearing and reflecting to bear upon practice; only then does one gain true benefit.

[The Three Wisdoms] First, the wisdom of hearing: the wisdom born from seeing and hearing the sutras and teachings. Second, the wisdom of reflection: the wisdom born from pondering the principles. Third, the wisdom of cultivation: the wisdom born from practice. The first two wisdoms are scattered wisdoms, serving as the conditions that give rise to the wisdom of cultivation; the wisdom of cultivation is a wisdom of concentration, which has the function of severing delusion and realizing truth.

blocks.text: Appendix: On Rebuilding the Life-Release Pond at Nanxun Jile Temple

inline.s: The matter of abstaining from killing and releasing life is shallow and easy to perceive; the principle of abstaining from killing and releasing life is deep and hard to understand. If one does not understand the principle, though one may carry out the act, the mind can never become sincerely compassionate; the merit and blessings of its field of merit likewise become shallow and slight in keeping with the measure of one’s mind. Should one meet with the obstruction and slander of those who do not understand, one may well be turned about by them, and with that a whole good heart is extinguished. Therefore, without avoiding a surplus of words, I set forth its meaning, so that creatures alike may bathe in compassionate kindness and human relationships may each cultivate their well-being. With the most earnest and profound benevolence we extinguish the retribution of killing for self and other, together reaching the realm of longevity and sharing the joy of a full life. Still further, I pray that this merit be dedicated to the Western Land, so that one may forever emerge from the wheel of transmigration, soaring above the three realms, to be a disciple of Amitābha Buddha and a good companion in the great ocean of beings. May the reader pay heed to this.

Originally, the one-thought mind-nature of the creatures of water and land is, at once, not the least different from that of the Buddhas of the three times. But because the power of karma from past evil deeds has obscured the wondrous brightness, it cannot manifest, and they sink into other classes of beings. Thus their knowledge is mean and inferior: apart from seeking food and escaping death, they know nothing at all. It is like a great precious bronze mirror that for kalpas has been veiled in dust. Not only is it wholly without brightness — even the mirror’s own bronze substance does not appear, and it is just like a useless object. Suddenly it meets a wise person who knows that this is a precious mirror endowed with the boundless light that illumines heaven and earth. He therefore polishes it day after day: at first the mirror’s substance is slightly revealed, next its brightness gradually shines forth, and when the polishing is carried to the utmost, the light that illumines heaven and earth is manifested in its entirety. Only then does the unwise person come to treasure it and regard it as a supreme jewel. One must know that this light the mirror has possessed from the very beginning — it is not obtained from the polishing. Although it is inherently possessed, if there were no condition of polishing, then from kalpa to kalpa there would be no day when it would shine.

The mind-nature of all the beings of the six realms, human and divine, is entirely like this. From beginningless time defilement and karma have obscured it, so that the wondrous brightness inherently present cannot be displayed; deluded and turning against their true nature, they create the karma of birth and death. The Great One Awakened, the World-Honored One, knows that the one-thought mind-nature of all sentient beings is the same as that of the Buddha. For this reason, by various expedient means, he speaks the Dharma in accordance with their capacities, universally causing beings to cultivate the path of precepts, concentration and wisdom, so that, by severing defilement and karma, they may recover what is originally theirs, perfect their merit and wisdom, and realize the Dharma body. He also causes the people of the world to arouse a mind of compassion and abstain from killing and release life. This is because I and all sentient beings are all within the wheel of transmigration. From beginningless time we have been born and reborn one another in turn, and killed one another in turn. They have each in turn been my father, my mother, my elder and younger brothers, my elder and younger sisters, my sons and daughters; and I too have in turn been their father, mother, brothers, sisters, sons and daughters. They indeed, by the power of their evil karma, whether in the human realm or in other classes, have repeatedly suffered my slaughter; and I too, by the power of my evil karma, whether in the human realm or in other classes, have repeatedly suffered their slaughter. Through long kalpas, mutually giving birth and mutually killing, there is no end to it. Ordinary people do not know this; the Tathāgata sees it clearly. Now, having been taught and knowing this for oneself, if one does not reflect on it there is nothing to say, but when one does reflect on it, one is overcome with a shame and compassion beyond bearing!

Now I have been fortunate to inherit the merit and good karma of past lives and am born in the human realm. Surely I ought to dissolve enmity and loosen the knots, abstain from killing and release life, and cause all sentient beings to each gain their proper place. Moreover, for their sake I recite the Buddha and dedicate the merit to the Pure Land, so that they may attain deliverance. Even if, their karma being heavy, they cannot be reborn there immediately, I shall rely upon this compassionate and virtuous merit and earnestly seek, at the end of life, to be reborn in the Western Land. Once reborn there, one at once transcends the ordinary and enters the holy, ends birth and death, forever escapes transmigration, and gradually realizes the Buddha fruit.

Moreover, loving creatures and releasing life — the ancient sages and worthies all practiced this. Thus the Book of Documents has the passage, “Birds, beasts, fish and turtles all are thus,” meaning that birds, beasts, fish and turtles should all be allowed to follow their natural inclinations, free from the suffering of being killed and the terror of being startled; and King Wen’s grace reached even to dry bones — how much the more to creatures possessed of consciousness! As for Jianzi releasing the turtle-dove, Zichan keeping the fish, the Marquis of Sui rescuing the snake, and Yang Bao saving the sparrow — these are indeed the impartial hearts of the sages and worthies who regard all alike, yet they did not yet know that all moving, breathing beings possess the Buddha-nature, that they rise and sink in mutual turn becoming now enemies and now kin, and the principle that in the future they are certain to realize Buddhahood. When the great teaching came east, the causality of the three times and the truth that the mind-natures of sentient beings and of the Buddha are equal and undifferentiated were greatly revealed to the world. Every great sage and worthy has taken abstaining from killing and releasing life as the foundation for turning back the calamity of slaughter to cultivate the fruit of blessing, for stilling the weapons of war and joyfully enjoying a full life.

The ancients said, “If you would know the calamity of weapons in the world, you must hearken to the sound at the butcher’s door in the dead of night.” And again, “If you would have the world free of the calamity of weapons, it is only if sentient beings do not eat flesh.” From this one knows that abstaining from killing and releasing life is the good remedy for saving the world by plucking up its roots. Therefore the Great Master of Tiantai bought more than sixty places along the riverbanks and streams of Linhai, extending over four hundred li, as a life-release pond. He requested that an imperial edict erect a stele forbidding fishing and catching; and those who secretly fished would readily bring misfortune upon themselves. Even down to the Zhenguan era of the Tang it was still so. In the second year of the Qianyuan era of Tang Suzong, an edict was issued to all the prefectures of the empire to each establish a life-release pond, and the emperor commanded Yan Zhenqing to compose the stele inscription and to write it in his own hand. It said, “Our sovereign takes the whole world as a pond, and all within the realm receive blessing; relying upon the sustaining power of the dhāraá¹‡ī, he exhausts the sea of affliction and the ford of birth and death. Compared with ancient times, what could ever resemble this?”

Someone says: Widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are to be found everywhere; why do you not relieve them, and instead eagerly busy yourself with creatures of another class with whom you have no concern? Are not the urgent and the important thus reversed?
